summary: This informational memo describes a MAPOS extension, the Node Switch Protocol, for automatic node address assignment.

plainLanguage.summary: NSP lets a MAPOS node ask its connected switch for an HDLC address. The node repeats the request if no assignment arrives and periodically checks that the address is still valid.

questions: what is the node switch protocol
how does a mapos node get an address
subtitle: How a MAPOS node asks its switch for the HDLC address it should use.

tldr.problem: Every MAPOS node needs an HDLC address associated with its switch port. Assigning and maintaining those addresses by hand can lead to inconsistencies.
tldr.mechanism: The Node Switch Protocol (NSP) sends an address request to the local switch control processor. The switch replies with an assignment or a rejection, and later requests act as keep-alives.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2173 describes an informational MAPOS version 1 extension. It reduces address configuration work but does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2173 is an Informational memo published in June 1997. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: MAPOS Nodes and Their Addresses
sections.content:
MAPOS carries network datagrams in High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC) frames over SONET or SDH links. A SONET switch forwards each frame using its address, and each node needs a unique address within that switch.

RFC 2173 adds the Node Switch Protocol (NSP) to MAPOS version 1. NSP lets a node retrieve its HDLC address from the switch to which it is connected.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS sends network data in frames over SONET or SDH links. Each node needs an address that lets its switch identify where to forward a frame.

sections.title: The MAPOS Address
sections.content:
A MAPOS address is 8 bits long. Its least significant bit is always 1, marking the end of the address field. For unicast, the most significant bit is 0 and the remaining bits identify the connected port; address 0x01 is reserved for the local switch control processor.

In a multi-switch network, a unicast address contains a switch number and a port number. Broadcast and multicast use the most significant bit set to 1; for broadcast, all the other address bits are 1.
sections.plainLanguage: A MAPOS address is 8 bits, and its last bit is always 1. For a normal message, the other bits identify a port, or a switch and port in a multi-switch network.

sections.title: Requesting and Checking an Address
sections.content:
After a node connects and receives a valid SONET signal, it sends an NSP address request to destination 0x01, the local control processor. If the processor can assign an address, it replies with an assignment packet. If it cannot, it sends a reject packet. A request uses command value 1, an assignment uses 2, and a rejection uses 3.

If no assignment arrives within 5 seconds, the node retransmits its request until it succeeds. It MUST also send a request every 30 seconds to verify its address. The switch treats these requests as keep-alives and assumes the node is down after more than 90 seconds without one, or after detecting a SONET signal failure.
sections.plainLanguage: A node sends a request to the switch control processor, which assigns an address or rejects the request. The node repeats an unanswered request after 5 seconds and checks its address every 30 seconds.

sections.title: NSP Packet and Special Connections
sections.content:
An NSP packet contains a 32-bit command field and a 32-bit address field. A request should put zeroes in its address field. An assignment carries the assigned address in the least significant byte and zeroes in the remaining bytes; the address field in a rejection is undefined.

NSP also covers a direct point-to-point connection without a switch and a loop-back connection from a node's output to its input. In either case, the responding node assigns address 0x03. Both nodes in a point-to-point connection therefore use that address, which the RFC says is acceptable for that case.
sections.plainLanguage: Each NSP packet has a command and an address field. For a direct connection between two nodes, or a loop-back test, the reply assigns address 0x03.

sections.title: Security and Document Status
sections.content: The RFC says that security issues are not discussed. It describes NSP as an extension for automatic address assignment and does not define an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not discuss security. It provides information about an address-assignment extension, not an Internet standard.
